newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees rules on irradiated food.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees rules on irradiated food.

text.p: European Union internal market ministers reached political agreement on Wednesday on the sensitive issue of treating foodstuffs with ionizing radiation to increase their shelf life and to remove pests.
The directive paves the way for free trade in such foodstuffs in the EU, provided they are included on a list which has to be agreed by member states and the European Parliament.

The immediate impact of the new directive will be limited, however, as the initial list of irradiated products which can be marketed freely across the EU will include only dried aromatic herbs, spices and vegetable seasonings.
Such products are often contaminated or infested with organisms harmful to human health.
The idea is then to expand the number of foodstuffs. The European Commission must propose a final list by 2002.
Food irradiation is a physical method of processing food like heat treatment, freezing or additives.
EU diplomats said the compromise solution sought to strike a balance between those countries wanting free trade in all irradiated foodstuffs now and those which were sceptical.
Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Austria -- with strong consumer interest groups -- are generally seen as being suspicious of this way of treating food.
The ministers agreed on two sets of legislation, one laying down general provisions on irradiation and another which established the initial list of foodstuffs.
EU countries would be able to keep national bans on all foodstuffs or food ingredients not included on the list until the EU has agreed a final list, even if they are allowed elsewhere.
However, there was some concern that such a ban may be challenged on the grounds it goes against EU rules on free trade. Partly for this reason, Italy made clear it would vote against the proposal.
Also under the directive, all ingredients treated with ionizing radiation must be mentioned on the labelling.
Food irradiation would be allowed only if there is a reasonable technological need to do it, if it is beneficial for consumers and if there is no health hazard.
